A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DOTS and rollout-replay research. Their main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support a reliable comparison without material reading gaps.

before.justification: v1 reports original RL fine-tuning experiments across six model-dataset combinations, training-time measurements, difficulty-prediction results, and appendix ablations.

after.justification: v2 retains original experimental results and adds science-domain evaluation, longer training runs, AIME diagnostics, and an empirical check of its theoretical assumption.

M1.justification: Appendix A.1 adds a reference-rollout reuse variant: rollouts from reference questions near difficulty 0.5 are incorporated into training. Algorithm 1 also adds a buffer-availability guard. The central attention predictor, calibration, difficulty targeting, and FIFO replay design remain intact.

E1.justification: Alongside the retained mathematical training datasets and four evaluation benchmarks, v2 adds STEM training on SCP-25K and evaluation on MMLU physics, chemistry, and biology questions. Appendix D.4 also adds an auxiliary AIME 24 evaluation, without incorporating it into the main four-benchmark average.

E2.justification: The comparator membership is retained: original GRPO with uniform sampling, the external-difficulty curriculum, and frozen off-the-shelf embeddings. The curriculum comparison moves from v1 Appendix F.2 to v2 Section 5.4 and uses GPT-4o-mini in both. Random in the revised plots denotes the existing uniform-sampling baseline.

E3.justification: v2 adds 100-step comparisons for two retained model-dataset combinations, AIME avg@8 evaluation every ten training steps, and a covariance check using 512 questions with eight rollouts each. The main 60-step protocol remains; the newly stated mini-batch size and gradient-update counts clarify existing settings rather than establish a changed main protocol.

E4.justification: New analyses examine persistence of gains over 100 training steps, the theorem's weak-dependence assumption, and AIME evaluation instability. Appendix A.1 also briefly reports reference-solution embedding and reference-rollout reuse checks. Existing component, reference-size, and external-curriculum analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Figure 3 newly reports 95% confidence intervals across three independent runs for the main performance comparisons. v1 provides no corresponding run-based uncertainty, although its prediction tables already report standard deviations across training steps. This establishes expanded uncertainty reporting, not a known increase from a specified earlier run count.

E6.justification: Table 1 revises five of six result rows: total time saved changes from 32.15% to 26.25% for Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B on MATH and from 24.94% to 48.03% for Qwen2.5-Math-7B on DeepScaleR. Average savings change from 38.8% to 40.7%. Science, AIME, longer-run, covariance, and reference-reuse findings are added; predictor correlation results remain unchanged.

T1.justification: v1's proof assumes independence between rewards and likelihood gradients. v2 Appendix B introduces an explicit covariance correction and a weak-dependence assumption allowing that correction to be neglected. It also adds a derivation for independent correctness-plus-format rewards. These substantively revise the assumptions and mathematical scope supporting the retained 50% difficulty claim.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction revise the claimed training-time reduction from 25-65% to 23-62%. The central contributions remain adaptive difficulty prediction, difficulty-targeted selection, and rollout replay; the conclusion retains the same overall message.

C2.justification: v2 adds an explanation that changing difficulty promotes sample diversity and prevents overfitting, interprets the science experiment as broader applicability, and discusses when DOTS overhead is offset by faster convergence. Appendix A.1 adds limitations concerning unavailable reference solutions and reference-rollout overhead while retaining the earlier limitations.

D1.justification: Section 5.1 and Table 4 newly specify mini-batches of 64, eight gradient updates per training step, and 480 updates for the main runs. v2 also specifies an 8,192-question SCP training subset and training a science difficulty predictor. The code URL is unchanged and moves from v1 Appendix A to the abstract.

R1.justification: v2 more explicitly credits traditional experience replay as motivation and broadens the appendix novelty statement from unexplored rollout replay in GRPO to unexplored replay in LLM RL fine-tuning. The 51-entry bibliography is retained, but several citation positions in v2 are unresolved.

P1.justification: v2 standardizes terminology, makes localized explanatory edits, moves the existing curriculum case study into Section 5.4, and relocates the code disclosure to the abstract. It also updates the conference header and adds an acknowledgment. The main section sequence and most existing prose remain recognizable.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn with an explicit iteration loop, and Figure 3 gains error bars and revised axes and legends. The existing curriculum plots are merged with the new science plot in Figure 6. v2 adds the AIME table and extended-training plots; Figures 9-10 redisplay existing comparisons using alternative step/time axes.

improvement.justification: Newly reported three-run confidence intervals, longer-training checks, and science-domain results strengthen the empirical support, while clearer update-count documentation helps reproducibility. The net gain is limited by unresolved citations, the 100-step experiment's inconsistent description as 600 gradient steps, and the revised proof's exact optimality claim after a nonzero covariance term is neglected.
